title: China's export control framework: domestic developments and international positioning
date_evidence: Topical Backgrounder by Giovanna Maletta and Fei Su, published 29 April 2026 — SIPRI commentary byline.
key_claim: Since 2020 China has built a comprehensive export-control system that mirrors elements of the US model (end-user blacklists, an Unreliable Entity List) and asserts extraterritorial application to foreign entities re-exporting Chinese-origin items; in October 2025 it made certain critical-material exports subject to extraterritorial controls, suspended for a year shortly afterwards under the Trump-Xi agreement; in April 2026 China adopted a new regulation on industrial and supply-chain security enabling export controls as countermeasures; in January 2026 it banned dual-use and critical-material exports to Japanese military end-users.
notes: SIPRI Topical Backgrounder, authors Giovanna Maletta and Fei Su, byline 29 April 2026. Verified via WebFetch; full text read.

publisher: Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS)
title: Reining in the Export Control Arms Race
date_evidence: CSIS Commentary by Koren, Kennedy, Luck, Mazzocco — 'Published April 10, 2026' byline.
key_claim: Export controls have evolved from a narrow, multilateral non-proliferation tool into a broad instrument of economic statecraft, deployed unilaterally and negotiated as bargaining chips; export controls were 'never treated as bargaining chips' historically. After the April 2025 US tariffs China added rare earths to its control list; a June 2025 truce gave way to a September US affiliates rule and, two weeks later, China's comprehensive extraterritorial rare-earth regime consistent with the US Foreign Direct Product rule; the late-October ceasefire suspended the US affiliates rule and China's de minimis, FDP and 50% rules for one year. A March 2026 CSIS survey found 56% of semiconductor and IT firms faced licence reviews averaging over 180 days and 54% reported lost business; in January 2026 Chinese exports of controlled products to Japan fell 43%.
notes: CSIS Commentary, authors Koren, Kennedy, Luck, Mazzocco, 'Published April 10, 2026'. Verified via WebFetch; full text read. Also the main counter-evidence source on the 'bargaining chip / credibility erosion' objection.

title: OECD Inventory of Export Restrictions on Critical Raw Materials 2026 / Critical raw materials face rising export restrictions
date_evidence: OECD press-release URL slug contains '/2026/04/' and OECD Inventory of Export Restrictions on Critical Raw Materials 2026 release announced April 2026 (cross-confirmed via WebSearch results referencing the April 2026 OECD release).
key_claim: Export restrictions cover up to 45% of global rare-earth exports, 47% of graphite and around 70% of cobalt and manganese; export restrictions on critical raw materials have risen roughly fivefold since 2009 and remain at historically high levels; China alone produces around 70% of global rare earths and graphite and more than 90% of germanium and magnesium.
notes: OECD Inventory of Export Restrictions on Critical Raw Materials 2026, released April 2026. title: China Expands Its Playbook: New Industrial Supply Chain and Counter-Extraterritoriality Regulations Create Direct Compliance Conflicts for Multinationals
date_evidence: Mayer Brown International Trade publication byline reads 'May 05, 2026'.
key_claim: On 7 April 2026 China's State Council issued the Regulations on Industrial and Supply Chain Security and on 13 April 2026 the Regulations on Countering Improper Extraterritorial Jurisdiction by Foreign States, both effective immediately; together they create a unified retaliatory framework with a 'malicious entity list' and a structural conflict in which routine compliance with US, UK and EU sanctions, export controls and forced-labour rules may itself trigger Chinese investigations, prohibition orders and countermeasures, with personal exposure for executives, in-house counsel and outside advisers.
notes: Mayer Brown International Trade publication, byline 'May 05, 2026'. Verified via WebFetch; full text read. Law-firm analysis (Tier 3) but the most detailed account of the April 2026 China regulations.

title: Global Trade Outlook and Statistics, March 2026 (Middle East conflict weighs further on slowing trade outlook)
date_evidence: WTO news release URL slug 'stat_19mar26_329_e.htm' encodes 19 March 2026; page dateline 'Global Trade Outlook and Statistics, March 2026' issued 19 March 2026.
key_claim: World merchandise trade volume grew 4.6% in 2025 and is forecast to slow to 1.9% in 2026; the negative impact of 2025 tariffs was smaller than predicted owing to suspensions, limited retaliation and exemptions; the share of world trade conducted on a most-favoured-nation basis stood at 72% by the end of February 2026, with MFN tariffs remaining the dominant framework governing international trade across most sectors.
notes: WTO Global Trade Outlook and Statistics March 2026; news release dated 19 March 2026. Data confirmed via WebSearch. Used for the counter-argument (tariffs still dominate most trade) and fragmentation context.

title: Exposure of Major Chinese-Linked Chip Smuggling Operations Shows Limits of Industry Self-Policing
date_evidence: FDD analysis URL slug '/analysis/2026/03/20/' encodes 20 March 2026; corroborated via WebSearch snippet referencing the FDD March 20, 2026 brief on chip smuggling.
